READING PASSAGE 2 
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading 
Passage 2 on pages 6 and 7. 
 
An Australian Tree Abroad 
The impact of the eucalyptus tree in Portugal 
 
A 
The eucalyptus is an iconic Australian tree; there are more than 700 species and most of 
them are native to Australia. Some eucalyptus species have attracted attention from 
Horticulturists, global development researchers and environmentalists because these trees 
have a number of desirable traits. They are fast-growing sources of wood, producing oil 
that can be used for cleaning and for repelling insects. Eucalyptus have even been planted 
in areas where there is a need to drain swamps which pose health risks because of malaria-
carrying mosquitos. However, outside their natural Australian habitat, eucalyptus are both 
praised for their beneficial economic impact on poor populations, and criticised for being a 
water-consuming alien species. 
 
B 
In the late 18th century, as eucalyptus became more well known for their ornamental and 
medicinal qualities, they were introduced into some European countries, one of which was 
Portugal. By the 19th century there was almost no native woodland left in Portugal, and 
eucalyptus were seen as a good tree to build up Portugal’s forests. For example, for two 
decades, beginning in 1866, some 35,000 eucalyptus were planted around the Portuguese 
university town of Coimbra in an effort to control devastating soil erosion caused by 
excessive tree felling. Today, just a short drive from Coimbra, in Vale de Canas, a sea of 
eucalyptus extends to the horizon in all directions. The tallest tree in Europe can be found 
in the Vale de Canas and, ironically, this tree is a eucalyptus that was planted in a deep, 
foggy gorge around 120 years ago. It is a Eucalyptus di versicolor (karri) standing 72 
metres in height, and next to it is another native Australian tree, an Araucaria bidwillii 
(Bunya pine), which is the tallest example of the species ever recorded. 
 
C 
A century after the planting of the eucalyptus near Coimbra, Scandinavian timber 
companies began buying up vast parcels of Portuguese land to grow plantations of 
Eucalyptus globulus, or blue gum eucalyptus, to pulp for paper. The planting of trees on 
the land local people had used for generations led to the breakdown of financial and 
trading systems in villages where many people still relied on communal farming. In fact 
special laws were created to allow for the expansion of the eucalyptus plantings. ‘Portugal 
was not in a position to guard against those projects,’ says Pedro Bingre, the regional 
director of Portugal’s major environmental group, Quercus. The group was named after the 
native cork oak tree (Quercus Suber), which is in steady decline throughout Portugal partly 
due to the proliferation of eucalyptus. Bingre explained that by the early 1970s Portugal 
needed the money that the plantation projects would generate to boost the weakening 
economy.

7 
 
D 
Now, the exotic blue gum eucalyptus is the most abundant tree in Portugal, covering about 
7% of the land. A walk through Vale de Canas beneath the towering blue gum eucalyptus 
might feel familiar to an Australian, apart from one significant difference Portuguese blue 
gum eucalyptus forests are deathly quiet, whereas Australian blue gum eucalyptus forests 
are home to a host of species such as koalas. ‘Our fauna can’t feed on it; they can’t find 
refuge in it. Our insects can’t eat eucalyptus, so there are no birds,’ says Bingre. ‘We 
should introduce koalas. At least there would be something cute to look at.’ 
 
E 
Plantation blue gum eucalyptus are grown in rotation periods of 12 years, during which 
time the undergrowth is cleared at least twice. ‘In a native oak forest you’d find, in one 
hectare of woodland, at least 70 or 80 species of plant,’ says Bingre. ‘In a eucalyptus 
forest, you would hardly find more than 15.’ Eucalyptus are not just found in plantations; 
now, in many parts of Portugal, they grow in the wild. However, it was the drying up of 
village water supplies as a result of the demand for water from the plantation eucalyptus 
that sparked a groundswell of feelings against the ‘eucalyptusisation’ of Portugal. ‘Ever 
since the mid-1970s people have been protesting,’ explains Bingre. 
 
F 
Paulo Bernardo de Andrade, one of Quercus’s co-founders, was among the original 
plantation opponents. ‘One of the most effective protests was to pull out the baby trees. 
We used to chain ourselves to the machinery used to excavate the earth, too.’ He smiles 
ruefully. ‘That was the 1970s. Things have changed.’ Today, Andrade sees education as 
Quercus’s best strategy, helped by evolving technology. He adds that currently Brazil turns 
out twice as much wood pulp per hectare as the Portuguese wood pulp industry, which 
only remains financially viable because of the high cost of transporting wood pulp from 
Brazil to Europe. Meanwhile, demand for paper is declining worldwide as people are 
buying fewer newspapers and magazines. He goes on to say ‘Some studies say that in 20 
or 30 years’ time there won’t be enough demand for pulp to justify these huge plantations 
of eucalyptus, which will be a new problem for us. It’s very unlikely that the pulp-
producing companies will be willing to convert their plantation forest back into native 
forest. It would be very expensive.’ 
 
G 
Another factor that is threatening native cork oaks is that cork, which is harvested from the 
bark of mature trees, is no longer in such demand because screw-top wine caps have 
largely replaced traditional cork stoppers in wine bottles. In addition, eucalyptus are 
particularly hardy; they are capable of regrowing up to three times after harvesting. In 
many parts of Portugal eucalyptus already grow wild. To local environmentalists, the 
eucalyptus is to Portugal what the rabbit is to Australia – an introduced pest.

Questions 20 and 21 
Choose TWO letters, A-E 
Write the correct letters in boxes 20 and 21 on your answer sheet 
Which TWO of the following statements are true of the Scandinavian timber companies? 
 
 
A 
They paid local farmers for the use of their land. 
 
B 
Their plantations destroyed traditional rural economies. 
 
C 
They provided pulp to the Portuguese paper-making industry. 
 
D 
They chose Portugal because the climate suits tree growing. 
 
E 
They benefited from Portuguese legislation.

Questions 22 and 23

Which TWO of the following statements represent Paulo Bernardo de Andrade’s opinion of 
Portugal’s pulp industry? 
 
 
A 
New technology is making it more financially viable. 
 
B 
It is more productive than the Brazilian pulp industry. 
 
C 
It continues to be competitive as a result of the distance between Brazil and 
Europe. 
 
D 
If it fails, the future of the eucalyptus plantations will be uncertain. 
 
E 
It should change to the production of cork. 
 
Questions 24 – 26 
 
Complete the summary below. 
 
Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer. 
 
Write your answer in boxes 24-26 on your answer sheet. 
 
Blue gum eucalyptus in Portugal 
In Australia, the native fauna, for example 24 ............ live successfully off the blue gum 
eucalyptus. This is not the case in Portugal where, as Bingre points out, the insects reject 
eucalyptus as a food source, and without insects to feed on, 25 ............ are absent from 
Portuguese blue gum eucalyptus forests. In addition, undergrowth is removed regularly. Bingre 
argues that this is why there are far fewer species of plant in each 26 ............ of a eucalyptus 
forest than in a forest of the native cork oaks. Eucalyptus growing outside plantations are 
considered by environmentalists to be a pest and should never have been introduced.
